claims.text: A tungsten-based high-entropy alloy can serve as an intermediate material in a plasma-facing reactor component.
Conventional processing yields a homogeneous tungsten-based HEA intermediate-layer microstructure.
Adding a few weight percent copper and applying tailored post-processing will produce Cu-rich nanoprecipitates in the tungsten-based HEA.
The induced Cu-rich nanoprecipitates will be coherent and well dispersed.
Plasma-facing reactor intermediate layers experience cyclic thermal and mechanical loading at roughly 500–1000 °C.
Copper has high intrinsic thermal conductivity.
Cu-rich nanoprecipitates provide additional heat-conduction pathways through the HEA.
The additional conduction pathways lower the intermediate layer's thermal resistance.
Coherent bonding and fine precipitate dispersion help maintain the mechanical strength of the alloy.
Copper modification will increase effective thermal conductivity by approximately 10–20% relative to the undoped baseline.
The copper-modified HEA will retain yield strength comparable to that of the undoped baseline under reactor operating conditions.
The copper-modified HEA will retain ductility comparable to that of the undoped baseline under reactor operating conditions.
The comparison baseline is an undoped, conventionally processed tungsten-based HEA intermediate layer.
The anticipated improvement is limited to tungsten-based HEAs under the specified high-temperature cyclic-loading conditions.
The precipitate distribution may coarsen or become phase-unstable during extended reactor exposure.
The effects of the intervention in other alloy systems or under prolonged extreme irradiation are unverified.
